URL shortener

People paste a long web address and get back a short one. Millions of other people then tap that short link, so reading is almost everything. Keep every tap fast, and never lose a link. Practise this easy system design problem for free, with no sign-up.

Play this problem

The brief

People paste a long web address and get back a short one. Millions of other people then tap that short link, so reading is almost everything. Keep every tap fast, and never lose a link.

Think of a link shortener like Bitly.

Users, scale and requirements

Who uses it
50 million people a month
Audience in plain numbers
50,000,000 people per month
Normal peak
≈ 5,000 requests per second
Request mix
Read: 99%; Write: 1%
Speed for 99 of 100 requests
Read: ≈ 200 ms; Write: ≈ 200 ms
Successful requests
99.9%
Data safety
No acknowledged write may be lost.
Monthly budget
≈ $12,000
Data at rest
≈ 1.5 TB
Where users are
North America: 70%; Europe: 30%
Home region
North America
Waiting deadlines
Read: 900 seconds; Write: 3,600 seconds

≈ marks an approximation, just as in the game. Waiting deadlines measure the age of queued work and are separate from interactive response time.

  • Short codes are 7 characters. Each stored link uses about 0.5 KB including its metadata (approx.).
  • About 20 new links a second on average (≈ 50 million a month, approx.).
  • One app server handles about 1,000 requests a second (approx.).

Questions that shape the design

Can a short link change after it is made?

No. A link never changes once created, so saved answers never go out of date and caching is safe.

How many people tap a link compared with people who make one?

About 99 taps for every 1 new link. This is a read-heavy system.

Do we count clicks live?

No. Click counts can arrive a few minutes late. The redirect itself must be fast.

The traffic day

Consumer traffic, busiest in the evening. The clock covers 00:00 to 24:00 in the home region. Events add pressure on top of that normal traffic.

  1. 19:30 · Viral spike

    A post blows up. Traffic climbs to several times normal within minutes.

    Traffic reaches 3 times the scheduled load; rises over 600 seconds, holds for 3,600 seconds and eases over 3,600 seconds.

  2. 12:10 · Cache stampede

    The cache empties (restart, purge, mass expiry) and every request rushes to the database at once.

    Recovery window: ≈ 300 seconds.

What a strong design has to handle

  • One server handles about 1,000 requests a second. At 5,000 that is 5 servers with no spare room, so plan for about 6 or more (the 3 from the intro is not enough here). What happens when a link goes viral?
  • A longer cache time means more hits and less cost. Links never change, so an hour or a day is safe here.
  • Collapsing misses stops a thousand people asking for the same cold link from hitting the database together.

Make a prediction, run a full traffic day, then compare the result. The in-game editorial opens after a finished day and includes measured reference designs.
